what_it_does: A crystal oscillator is a tiny chip that ticks at an exact, stable frequency (32.768 kHz is the standard for real-time clocks in watches and embedded devices). These oscillators need to draw extremely little power—normally 10 to 100 nanowatts—because they run continuously off tiny coin-cell batteries. This paper presents an ultra-low-power oscillator (0.36 nanowatts, roughly 200 times lower than existing designs) that uses a clever feedback technique: instead of continuously driving the crystal at full amplitude, it injects brief pulses timed to the crystal's natural motion, much like pushing a child on a swing once per cycle to keep it moving. The innovation is that the oscillator reliably starts up on its own without needing a separate start-up circuit, making it simpler and more robust against electrical noise.
